strengths: Fills a clear gap: First benchmark for end-to-end closed-loop materials discovery, addressing the iterative nature of real discovery vs. static predictive benchmarks
Well-designed modular framework: Composable architecture via YAML configuration enables systematic ablations, component isolation, and reproducible comparisons of diverse strategies
Discovery-centric evaluation metrics: AF, EF, and AUDC appropriately measure sample efficiency for multi-minima search rather than predictive accuracy
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Systematic comparison across 30 systems and three complexity levels with clear ablations showing component contributions
Valuable scaling insights: Demonstrates that planning and agentic methods become increasingly important for larger search spaces and tighter stability thresholds, with practical implications
High reproducibility standards: Code release, YAML-based configurations, explicit pseudocode, seed/hardware specification, and configuration file versioning
Extensible framework design: Abstracts oracle interface allowing future substitution of DFT/experimental oracles; supports both modular pipelines and agentic systems with tool use
Honest limitations discussion: Authors transparently acknowledge MP-20 bias, MLIP limitations, and narrow chemical scope; appropriate impact statement on autonomous systems
weaknesses: Critical oracle and dataset bias: Both generators (Chemeleon) and MLIP oracle are trained on MP-20, creating shared inductive biases that may artificially simplify discovery relative to real materials discovery; undermines realism of efficiency claims

Surrogate error dependence: Results critically depend on MLIP quality; Figure 5 shows MLIP rankings degrade at realistic (0.01 eV/atom) stability thresholds, but primary results use 0.1 eV/atom without justifying this choice
Limited chemical scope: Only inter-metallic systems evaluated; no oxides, sulfides, or other important material classes; generalizability to diverse chemistries unclear

Artificial experimental constraints: Small query budget (50 queries vs. hundreds/thousands in real discovery), initial materials from Materials Project provide unrealistic prior knowledge, stability thresholds appear somewhat arbitrary

Incomplete agentic systems evaluation: Only one LLM model (GPT-5.1) and one orchestrator implementation tested; API dependency raises reproducibility concerns; no comparison with classical optimization methods (Bayesian optimization, active learning) despite citing them

Statistical rigor gaps: No significance testing between methods, only 5 episodes per system, no multiple comparison correction, some results have large error bars; acceleration factor undefined case (set to budget) is arbitrary
Single agentic implementation: LLM Orchestrator AF (5.4) lower than Chemeleon+MLIP (6.4) yet claimed competitive; only one LLM and tool set (7 tools) tested; unclear how limiting tool set design is
Inconsistent experimental conditions: MLIP selector generates 1024 structures vs. 32 for planners (different batch sizes); acknowledged but not adequately addressed, complicating fair comparison

Incomplete metric validation: Fixed pymatgen.StructureMatcher tolerances for novelty checking; sensitivity to tolerance choices not explored; acceleration factor treatment of zero-baseline cases is problematic

Dense presentation: Critical implementation details relegated to appendices; LLM components scattered across sections; some figures hard to read; real-world discovery workflows differ from 'select-generate-select' per-query workflow

strengths: Addresses a genuine gap in materials discovery benchmarking by enabling closed-loop evaluation instead of isolated static tasks
Well-designed modular and composable framework that enables systematic ablation of discovery components (planners, generators, filters, selectors) with reproducible YAML-based configuration
Comprehensive experimental design including multiple system complexities, multiple discovery strategies, multiple evaluation metrics with proper error bars and multiple episodes
Provides actionable empirical insights: generative model quality matters, MLIP selection is effective (AF=6.4), and planning importance scales with problem difficulty
Strong emphasis on reproducibility with promised code release and extensive implementation details in appendices
weaknesses: Conceptual novelty is limited: closed-loop discovery, active learning, and Bayesian optimization are well-established in materials science; problem formulation (Eq. 3) is straightforward; metrics are largely borrowed from prior work (Rohr et al. 2020, Merchant et al. 2023)

Critically flawed oracle setup that undermines benchmark realism: all generative models (Chemeleon), surrogates (MLIP/MACE), and oracle are trained on same MP-20 distribution; authors explicitly acknowledge this limitation creates 'shared distributional biases that may simplify discovery relative to real-world settings' but provide no DFT validation

Missing essential experimental comparisons: no Bayesian Optimization or uncertainty-aware active learning baselines (standard in materials discovery), no comparison to other agentic systems (Abhyankar et al. 2025 is cited but not compared), only weak baseline (random generator)

Shallow experimental analysis that validates intuitive expectations without deep insights: no investigation of why Random+LLM outperforms Chemeleon in larger systems, no analysis of LLM decision-making patterns, minimal discussion of efficiency-diversity tradeoffs, no timing/cost analysis

Severely limited evaluation scope: only inter-metallic systems (3-5 elements) tested, only one generative model (Chemeleon), only one oracle (MLIP), no evaluation on oxides/nitrides/other material classes, no DFT validation that discovered structures are actually thermodynamically stable

Insufficient statistical rigor: Table 1 claims 'statistically significant top results' without describing statistical test or p-values, many error bars overlap substantially yet relative rankings stated without significance testing, no multiple comparison correction applied

Problematic structure matching methodology uses pymatgen.StructureMatcher with default tolerances; different tolerances could substantially affect discovery counts; authors acknowledge this is a limitation but defer to future work

LLM orchestrator concerns: uses most capable model (GPT-5.1) making generalization unclear, adds API cost making it impractical for widespread use, unfair comparison to deterministic baselines given sophisticated tools and multi-step reasoning, unable to isolate what drives performance improvement

strengths: Addresses genuine gap in materials discovery benchmarking by enabling systematic evaluation of full closed-loop discovery pipelines rather than isolated components
Well-motivated problem formulation with clear mathematical framework (convex hull stability) appropriate for the domain
Modular and extensible framework design that supports diverse strategies from fixed pipelines to fully agentic LLM systems
Rigorous experimental evaluation across multiple dimensions: system complexities (ternary to quinary), varying difficulty levels (stability thresholds), and component ablations
Reproducibility-focused design with configuration-based experiments (Hydra), detailed implementation details, and explicit code release commitment
Important empirical findings showing adaptive planning becomes critical at larger system scales and surrogate models degrade at strict stability thresholds
Discovery-centric metrics (AF/EF) appropriately adapted to evaluate full pipeline efficiency rather than single-component performance
Clear presentation with effective motivation (Figure 2) and comprehensive appendices facilitating future adoption
weaknesses: Relies entirely on MLIP oracles despite claiming to support DFT/experimental validation; no demonstration with higher-fidelity oracles limits generality of findings
All components (Chemeleon, surrogates) trained on MP-20, introducing shared distributional biases that may simplify discovery relative to real-world settings
Missing comparison to classical Bayesian Optimization and Active Learning methods, which have strong track records in materials optimization problems
Limited scope: experiments restricted to inter-metallic systems with 50-query budgets; unclear how findings generalize to other material classes or larger discovery campaigns
LLM reproducibility concerns: single proprietary API provider (GPT-5.1) with undisclosed sampling parameters; long-term reproducibility compromised
Weak agentic system validation: LLM orchestrator underperforms best MLIP baseline on acceleration factor (5.4 vs 6.4) and doesn't convincingly answer central question about LLM efficacy
Incomplete sensitivity analysis: minimal exploration of stability threshold effects, structure matching tolerances, initial materials size, or generative model choices
Statistical significance testing absent; some reported differences (e.g., enhancement factors) appear marginal and lack formal significance tests or confidence intervals

strengths: Addresses genuine gap in materials discovery benchmarking by enabling first systematic evaluation of full closed-loop discovery pipelines with end-to-end feedback
Comprehensive and rigorous experimental evaluation across 30 chemical systems with multiple ablations, sensitivity analyses, and cross-family validation
Well-motivated framework design with clear desiderata (closed-loop evaluation, realistic search challenges, generality) and modular, extensible architecture
Thoughtful metric design with discovery-centric metrics (mSUN, AUDC, AF, EF) more appropriate than standard ML metrics for this domain
Excellent reproducibility with detailed implementation details, YAML-based configuration, comprehensive appendices, and promised code release
Clear scalability insights demonstrating that adaptive planning becomes increasingly important with system complexity and tight stability thresholds
Strong presentation with clear motivation, effective visualizations, and well-organized exposition making contributions accessible
weaknesses: Primarily a benchmark/infrastructure contribution with limited algorithmic novelty; empirical insights are somewhat expected (better models and planning help, MLIP errors matter near convex hull)
Distribution shift between training and evaluation: generators and oracles both trained on Materials Project data, creating artificial simplification where oracle is biased toward generator domain

MLIP oracle limitations: relative cheapness doesn't capture true cost structure of real discovery, oracle errors near convex hull undermine adaptive strategies, no systematic uncertainty quantification
Limited search budget (50 queries) and unclear scaling to realistic discovery campaigns with orders of magnitude more queries; composition planning is discrete not continuous
Incomplete baseline comparisons: no systematic Bayesian optimization, uncertainty sampling, or evolutionary algorithm baselines, limiting contextualization of LLM agent performance

Generalization questions: evaluation focuses on intermetallics (max 5 elements) with only supplementary chemistry family results; applicability to molecular discovery and larger high-entropy systems unclear

Limited exploration of agentic capabilities: LLM orchestrator uses simple ReAct with fixed tools, no investigation of more sophisticated agents with literature search, uncertainty quantification, or hierarchical reasoning
Lack of validation against real discovery outcomes: no evidence that MADE rankings align with actual experimental discoveries or that findings transfer beyond benchmark

strengths: Addresses a genuine gap in materials discovery benchmarking—existing benchmarks evaluate isolated tasks rather than closed-loop pipelines
Modular, extensible framework design with configuration-based reproducibility using Hydra and declarative YAML files
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple system complexities (ternary to quinary) with systematic ablation of pipeline components (planner, generator, selector)
Well-motivated presentation with clear problem formulation (Eqs. 1-3) and informative visualizations (Figures 1, 4, 5)
Practical contribution: flexible benchmark supporting both deterministic pipelines and agentic LLM systems
Extensive appendices with implementation details and diverse baselines (chalcogenides, halides, oxides) demonstrating generalization
weaknesses: Fundamental circular evaluation setup: oracle (MLIP), generators (Chemeleon), filters, and initial materials (H₀) all trained/derived from Materials Project, undermining claims about 'realistic discovery' when all components know the same landscape

Oracle uses MLIP surrogate rather than DFT; Figure 5 shows MLIP rankings fail at tighter stability thresholds (0.01 eV), and errors near convex hull are well-documented (Riebesell et al. 2025), limiting fidelity claims

Main empirical findings are largely unsurprising: generative models help (known), MLIP ranking accelerates discovery (known from Matbench Discovery), planning helps at scale (intuitive). LLM agent achieves AF=5.4 vs. Chemeleon+MLIP AF=6.4—within error bars, indicating a trade-off rather than clear advantage
Missing comparisons to established active learning and Bayesian optimization methods that are mentioned in related work but not benchmarked, limiting baseline completeness

Discovery metric definition is narrow: uses only thermodynamic stability (ε-threshold on convex hull) ignoring functional properties, metastable materials, and property diversity relevant to real materials discovery

LLM reproducibility concerns: prompts (Listings 2-3) are heavily engineered with domain knowledge; performance varies significantly across LLM providers (GPT 5.1 AF=5.4 vs. DeepSeek AF=3.6); unclear sensitivity to prompt wording

Questionable experimental design choices: query budget of 50 is small (real campaigns much longer), H₀ max 20 atoms/cell may not reflect realistic starting materials, stability threshold ε=0.1 eV appears arbitrary without justification

Statistical analysis lacking: error bars shown but no significance tests; several comparisons (e.g., Chemeleon vs. Chemeleon+Diversity) have overlapping error ranges; AF undefined when baseline finds zero structures (handled ad-hoc)

Limited methodological novelty: framework is essentially a standard gym-like environment with borrowed metrics; diversity planner (Eqs. 4-5) is relatively simple; main contribution is providing a benchmark rather than novel methods or insights

Generalization analysis incomplete: main results focus on intermetallics; additional chemistries in appendix show different behaviors (e.g., LLM planning fails on halides) without explanation; no ablation of H₀ size, oracle accuracy impact, or failure modes

strengths: Addresses a genuine gap in materials discovery benchmarking by enabling the first systematic closed-loop evaluation of end-to-end pipelines, moving beyond static component-level assessment

Comprehensive experimental design with proper ablations across multiple system complexities (ternary-quinary), chemical families (intermetallics, chalcogenides, halides, oxides), and diverse strategies from random search to agentic LLMs
Well-designed discovery-centric metrics (mSUN, AUDC, AF, EF) that capture both discovery efficiency and quality, extending the discovery acceleration paradigm to full pipelines

Modular, extensible framework enabling flexible composition of planners, generators, filters, and selectors; supported by clear pseudocode, YAML configuration management, and promised public code release
Clear technical formulation (Eqs. 1-3) with appropriate use of convex hull stability criterion and multi-minima search objective that properly captures materials discovery challenges
Reveals actionable insights including the brittleness of MLIP screening at tight stability thresholds and the increasing importance of adaptive planning as search spaces scale
Strong reproducibility practices with detailed implementation documentation, specific hyperparameters, multiple seeds, and cross-chemical validation
weaknesses: Significant limitation of using MLIP oracles rather than DFT or experimental validation: generators are trained on same Materials Project data, simplifying discovery relative to real settings and reducing real-world relevance

Limited methodological novelty—primarily integrates existing components (Chemeleon, MACE, convex hulls, LLM prompting) rather than proposing new discovery algorithms; key findings (adaptive planning matters more for harder problems) are somewhat expected

Small sample sizes (5 episodes per system, 50-query budget) yield large confidence intervals and unclear scalability to realistic scenarios; no comparison to classical active learning or Bayesian optimization baselines despite motivation
Reproducibility concerns with proprietary LLM (GPT 5.1) in main results; open-source models relegated to appendix limits accessibility; LLM prompt design strategy not fully transparent

Shallow analysis of why methods work: limited exploration of what enables LLM planning success or which components contribute to performance; minimal ablation on LLM's use of different information types
Stability threshold ε = 0.1 eV is treated as default despite Figure 5 showing strong dependence; guidance on threshold selection for practitioners is absent

Limited scope of evaluated strategies: only 3 planners, 2-3 generators, 2 selectors; no exploration of uncertainty quantification or information-theoretic acquisition functions; diversity planner uses naive Euclidean distance

Single-query assumption doesn't capture batched/parallel evaluation scenarios; convex hull stability is simplified (ignores kinetics, temperature dependence); some results affected by edge cases (baseline finding zero structures)
